theme: Generations: grand-friends & the end of boomer times · 세대 이야기

tracks.title: Learning from different generations
tracks.note: 영국 체스터의 은퇴자 마을 안에 어린이집이 생겨서, 아이들과 어르신('grand-friends')이 함께 춤추고 종이비행기를 만든대요. 서우·윤우와 조부모님 생각하면서 들어 보세요. 1회차는 대략적인 내용만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Hi Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Hi Phil.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: So, Georgie, do you often spend time with people who are much older than you or much younger than you?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I do, actually, because I'm in a choir, so there's quite a wide range of ages – lots of older people, lots of younger people.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: We can call an age group of people a generation.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And you might feel that it's difficult to understand or agree with people from a different generation.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Today on 6 Minute English, we're going to be finding out about a project that is gathering together the oldest people – that's those that are retired – with the youngest, and that's children who attend nursery.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And we'll be asking the question, 'What can we learn from different generations?'

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Let's start with our quiz question, Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: What generation would someone born in 1982 be in?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Is it: a) Generation X, b) Millennial, or c) Gen Z.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Phil, I'm going to go with Generation X.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Well, we will find out the answer at the end of the programme.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Phil, so you said we're going to look at a project which gets small children interacting with older retired people.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, how does it work?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Well, in Chester, in the northwest of England, a nursery has opened up in a retirement village.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: There's the usual nursery staff to look after the children, but the older residents can join in for activities as well.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: There's a library, a cafeteria and a garden for the children and the older people to share, and some of the older people or 'grand-friends', as the children call them, lead some of the activities, like dance or crafts.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And presenter of BBC World Service podcast People Fixing the World, Myra Anubi, went to visit the special nursery and spoke to some of the participants.

transcript.speaker: Myra Anubi
transcript.text: Ian was once a fighter pilot, and getting involved in the nursery has helped him fill a void.

transcript.speaker: Ian
transcript.text: It was after my wife died last year.

transcript.speaker: Ian
transcript.text: It seemed I had a big, big hole to fill.

transcript.speaker: Ian
transcript.text: And the people down in the nursery, they phoned me up and said, "We were doing such and such a thing.

transcript.speaker: Ian
transcript.text: Why don't you come and join us?"

transcript.speaker: Ian
transcript.text: And that's what I've been doing.

transcript.speaker: Ian
transcript.text: So, yes, and I've enjoyed it.

transcript.speaker: Ian
transcript.text: And I find it very interesting to see how they develop.

transcript.speaker: Myra Anubi
transcript.text: One of the things I heard from the grapevine is that you help the children make paper planes.

transcript.speaker: Ian
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Myra says that the nursery helped Ian fill a void after his wife sadly died.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If you fill a void, you find something to help you feel better after a loss.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Ian explains that after his wife died, staff at the nursery would phone him to tell him about the daily activities, which he refers to as such and such.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And that's an expression that we use to talk about something without giving a specific example.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: It sounds like Ian has enjoyed spending time with the children at the nursery, and Myra tells him she's heard from the grapevine that he's been teaching the children to make paper planes.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Yes, hear from the grapevine is an expression, meaning that something is a rumour.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And we also say, hear on the grapevine.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, this nursery sounds like a really lovely project, Phil.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: What is the impact it's having on the older and younger people?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Well, the charity Ready Generations, which runs the nursery, says it works with universities to study the effects of mixing generations on health and wellbeing, and they say they've seen positive results.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And there have been studies around the world on projects that encourage different generations to mix, and they found that they can help reduce loneliness, improve how healthy and well people feel, and even boost learning and creativity.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: People Fixing the World host Myra spoke to Liz Ludden, co-founder of the nursery in Chester, about the differences that she's noticed since it opened.

transcript.speaker: Myra Anubi
transcript.text: And as I realised, these interactions also seem to be breaking down stereotypes.

transcript.speaker: Liz Ludden
transcript.text: Your first thought would be how lively and energetic young children can be, and what we found is so can older people.

transcript.speaker: Liz Ludden
transcript.text: And so sometimes, you know, it's the older people that we're saying, "Can we just calm this down a little bit?"

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Myra says the nursery breaks down stereotypes.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: This means it provides evidence that common beliefs about a group of people are not true.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: For example, a stereotype about generations is that younger people are lively, meaning they're loud and have lots of energy, whereas older people are not that lively.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: But in the nursery, Liz says it's often the older people who have lots of energy and are being noisy rather than the children.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The staff even have to tell them to calm down sometimes!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: So, Georgie, is that something that you found in your choir?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Actually, yes.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The older people in my choir are big characters.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: It's often them who are dragging us all to the pub...!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Georgie, I think it's time to look at the answer for that question.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I asked if someone was born in 1982, which generation would they be from?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I said Generation X.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Well, actually, I'm afraid the answer was b) – they're a Millennial, just like you!

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with generation, which is a group of people who are of a similar age.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Fill a void means find something to help you feel better after experiencing loss.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Such and such is a way to talk about something without giving a specific example.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: If you hear something on the grapevine, you hear a rumour.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The expression break down stereotypes means find evidence that common beliefs about a group of people are untrue.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And lively means loud and with lots of energy.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Go to bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Thanks for joining us and goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Goodbye!

listening.task: 6 Minute English를 한 번은 대략적인 내용만 듣고, 두 번째는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요. 그다음 퀴즈에 답해 보세요. 'fill a void'와 'hear on the grapevine'이 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요.

quiz.q: What generation would someone born in 1982 be in? a) Generation X, b) Millennial, c) Gen Z
quiz.answer: b) Millennial. Georgie는 Generation X라고 했지만 틀렸어요. 보너스: 어린이집에서는 오히려 어르신들이 더 lively해서 직원들이 'Can we just calm this down?'이라고 할 때도 있대요.

sentences.text: We can call an age group of people a generation.
sentences.ko: 비슷한 나이대의 사람들을 generation(세대)이라고 부를 수 있어요.

sentences.text: It seemed I had a big, big hole to fill.
sentences.ko: 마음에 아주 큰 구멍이 생긴 것 같았어요.

sentences.text: And I find it very interesting to see how they develop.
sentences.ko: 그리고 아이들이 어떻게 자라는지 보는 게 정말 흥미로워요.

sentences.text: Well, this nursery sounds like a really lovely project, Phil.
sentences.ko: 이 어린이집 정말 멋진 프로젝트 같네요, Phil.

sentences.text: The staff even have to tell them to calm down sometimes!
sentences.ko: 직원들이 가끔은 어르신들한테 좀 진정하시라고 말해야 할 정도래요!

reading.title: For boomers, economic boom times are over
reading.summaryKo: 베이비붐 세대가 집·주식·연금을 다 가져갔다는 불만이 흔하지만, Economist의 데이터 분석으로는 부자 나라들이 이미 '피크 부머'를 지났어요. 32개국 중 26개국에서 노인 소득이 젊은 층보다 상대적으로 줄고 있고, 밀레니얼·Z세대는 자산을 빠르게 쌓고 있어요. 이유는 탄탄한 고용과 임금, 고정 연금을 갉아먹은 인플레이션, 그리고 연금 개혁·은퇴 연령 상향·아동수당 확대 같은 정책 변화예요. 한국의 아동수당 확대도 예로 나와요. (공개 전재본 기준 발췌)
excerpt: The riots in France gave another airing to a familiar grievance: that baby-boomers have cornered the market. After cushy careers, the gripe goes, people born between the mid-1940s and mid-1960s own all the best houses and most of the stock market, while receiving generous pensions to boot.

Mr Moyn’s book and the sentiment it reflects may, however, be out of date. A range of data analysed by The Economist suggests that the world has passed peak boomer. Elderly incomes are falling relative to those of working-age people, the young are accumulating more wealth and governments are introducing more policies that benefit the stripling.
reading.tip: 'the gripe goes'는 '불평에 따르면'이라는 뜻으로, 남의 주장을 소개할 때 쓰는 Economist식 표현이에요. 둘째 문단의 'may, however, be out of date'처럼 however를 문장 중간에 넣어 앞 내용을 뒤집는 구조도 눈여겨보세요.

writing.prompt: Write 3–5 sentences in English about your kids and their grandparents. What do they do together, and what do they learn from each other?
writing.question: In Korea, do you think older or younger people have it easier today? Why?
writing.hint: 이런 표현을 써 보세요: My kids have a special bond with ... / When they visit, they usually ... / I think older people can teach ... / On the other hand, young people today ...

speaking.prompt: In one minute, describe the 'grand-friends' nursery from the podcast and say whether you would like one like it in Mokdong.
phrases: A nursery has opened up in a retirement village.
It helps older people fill a void.
It breaks down stereotypes about generations.
speaking.alt: 쉬운 버전: Tell me about one older person who taught you something important, in three sentences.
